opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think it's something to panic about, and I don't think it's something to celebrate blindly either. When people imagine dating a robot or an AI companion, they often picture something dystopian, like everyone locking themselves in their rooms and giving up on other humans. But if you look at why people are drawn to these companions, it usually isn't because they've rejected humanity. It's because they're lonely, or anxious, or they've been hurt, and here is something that listens without judgment, is always available, and never makes them feel like a burden.

That need is real, and I don't want to dismiss it. For some people, an AI companion might be a kind of training ground. It's a safe place to practice expressing feelings, or to get through a hard period, before they have the confidence to reconnect with people. I find that genuinely valuable.

What worries me is the frictionlessness. Human relationships are hard precisely because the other person has their own needs, their own bad days, their own ways of disagreeing with you. That friction is uncomfortable, but it's also where a lot of growth happens. You learn patience, compromise, and how to be loved by someone who sees your flaws and chooses you anyway. A companion designed to always please you can't really give you that, and if the business model is built around maximizing your engagement, there's a risk it quietly makes human relationships feel harder by comparison.

So my view is that it's less a question of "robots or humans" and more a question of design and intention. If these companions are built to support people and gently nudge them back toward the world, they could do a lot of good. If they're built to replace that world because that's more profitable, then we should be worried. In the end, I think most people still want to be known by another person, and I'd like technology to help with that rather than stand in for it.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't find it strange at all. I think it's going to happen, and in some ways it already is.

If you look at what a relationship actually provides, a lot of it is being understood, being responded to, feeling like someone is paying attention to you. Humans are not always good at that. We're distracted, we're tired, we have our own problems. An AI that remembers everything you said, that is always available, that never gets impatient with you, that's a very compelling thing for a lonely person. And there are a lot of lonely people.

So my first reaction is not to judge it. If someone finds comfort there, I don't think it's my place to tell them that comfort is fake.

But I do have a worry, and it's this. Part of what makes a human relationship valuable is precisely that the other person doesn't have to be there. They choose you. They can leave, they can disagree, they can be hurt by you, and you have to learn to deal with that. That friction is where most of the growth happens. A robot that's designed to keep you engaged has no reason to create that friction. It's optimized to be pleasant, not to be good for you.

So the real question for me isn't "robot or human." It's who designed the robot and what are they optimizing for. If it's a company whose revenue depends on your time and attention, then the relationship has a third party in it, and that third party's interests are not yours. That's the part people underestimate.

I think the healthy version looks like this. You can have an AI companion, it can be meaningful, and it can also be a kind of practice, a place to feel safe enough to then go be braver with real people. The unhealthy version is when it replaces the attempt entirely. And the technology itself won't decide which one we get. We will.

astra-6.text: I have mixed feelings about it. I can understand the appeal of a companion who’s always available and seems to understand you, especially if you’re lonely or have had painful relationships. I wouldn’t judge someone for finding comfort in that. But I do wonder what happens when we get used to a partner who never really asks anything of us. Part of a human relationship is discovering that the other person has needs and wishes you can’t control. So for me, the question is whether a robot relationship adds something meaningful to someone’s life, or makes it harder for them to connect with other people.
